record.paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
record.original_question: How can federated learning become robust to non-malicious failures such as client reporting failures, secure-aggregation dropouts, data-pipeline bugs, and noisy model updates, while still respecting data-access restrictions that prevent direct inspection of raw client data?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a federated learning setting in which a central server coordinates training of a global model parameter $	heta \in \mathbb{R}^d$ across a population of clients $\{1,\dots,N\}$. In each communication round $t$, the server broadcasts the current iterate $	heta_t$ to a sampled subset $S_t \subseteq \{1,\dots,N\}$. Each selected client $i \in S_t$ holds a private local dataset $D_i$ and is expected to return a local update $g_{i,t}$ (e.g., a stochastic gradient or pseudo-gradient computed from $D_i$ and $	heta_t$). The server then aggregates the received updates, possibly via a privacy- or security-preserving mechanism (such as secure aggregation), and uses the aggregate to form $	heta_{t+1}$.

Assume the following non-malicious fault model (no adversarial behaviour):
(a) Reporting failures: each client independently drops out of round $t$ with probability $p_i$, in which case $g_{i,t}$ is missing.
(b) Secure-aggregation dropouts: when the number of successfully participating clients in a round falls below a threshold $	au$, the aggregate for that round is discarded.
(c) Data-pipeline corruption: with some probability $q$, an individual client's local dataset $D_i$ used in round $t$ is replaced by a corrupted version $	ilde{D}_i$ (e.g., from preprocessing bugs, label shifts, or feature scaling errors) producing a biased update $g_{i,t}$.
(d) Noisy updates: each reported update is further perturbed by zero-mean but possibly heavy-tailed noise $\eta_{i,t}$ with $\mathbb{E}\|\eta_{i,t}\|^2 \le \sigma^2$.

A crucial access restriction is imposed: the server may only observe (i) the aggregated updates produced by the secure aggregation primitive, plus (ii) low-bandwidth side information (such as scalar summaries that satisfy a fixed differential-privacy budget $(\varepsilon,\delta)$), but it may not inspect any raw client data $D_i$ nor any individual update $g_{i,t}$.

Design and analyse a federated training protocol $\mathcal{A}$ (specifying client-side update rules, server-side aggregation, dropout handling, and any allowable diagnostic queries respecting the access restriction) such that:

1. Under the fault model (a)–(d), the iterates produced by $\mathcal{A}$ converge in expectation to an $\varepsilon^*$-stationary point of the population objective $F(	heta) =  rac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \mathbb{E}_{D_i}[\ell(	heta;D_i)]$, with explicit dependence of $\varepsilon^*$ on $\{p_i\}$, $	au$, $q$, and $\sigma$.

2. $\mathcal{A}$ includes a debugging/monitoring procedure that, using only permissible aggregate or differentially private statistics, can detect with high probability whether systematic data-pipeline corruption (case (c)) is occurring and identify which round or client cohort is responsible, without violating the access restriction.

Provide either such a protocol with provable guarantees, or prove an impossibility result showing that no protocol satisfying the access restriction can simultaneously achieve (1) and (2) under the stated fault model.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is posed as an open research challenge in the federated learning literature, with no known general-purpose solution. While many partial advances exist (Byzantine-robust aggregation, secure aggregation with dropout tolerance, federated debugging tools), there is no comprehensive protocol with provable guarantees against the full non-malicious fault model under strict data-access restrictions.

status_evidence.title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
status_evidence.snippet: Lists robustness to non-malicious failures and developing general-purpose debugging methods as open problems for federated learning.
status_evidence.claim: The problem is explicitly identified as open in the federated learning research agenda.

status_evidence.title: A Field Guide to Federated Optimization
status_evidence.snippet: Surveys federated optimization and notes that handling client failures, stragglers, and silent data corruption without raw data access remains an active research direction.
status_evidence.claim: Subsequent surveys continue to list this as unresolved.
